(a) In General.—Section 1861(v)(1) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1395x(v)(1)) is amended by adding at the end the following new subparagraph: “(V) In determining such reasonable costs for skilled nursing facilities with respect to cost reporting periods beginning on or after October 1, 2005, the amount of bad debts otherwise treated as allowed costs which are attributable to the coinsurance amounts under this title for individuals who are entitled to benefits under part A and—“(i) are not described in section 1935(c)(6)(A)(ii) shall be reduced by 30 percent of such amount otherwise allowable; and“(ii) are described in such section shall not be reduced.”.  
    (b) Technical Amendment.—Section 1861(v)(1)(T) of such Act (42 U.S.C. 1395x(v)(1)(T)) is amended by striking “section 1833(t)(5)(B)” and inserting “section 1833(t)(8)(B)”.

fable.w: This section only amends the Medicare reasonable-cost formula to reduce allowable bad debt for skilled nursing facilities by 30 percent, and makes a technical cross-reference correction. A tempting reading is that it involves outside parties because it affects skilled nursing facilities and beneficiaries, but it gives them no role in any federal decision. There is no comment period, rulemaking, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside entities, or right to sue.

opus.w: The section sets a fixed rule for how Medicare reimburses skilled nursing facility bad debts: a 30 percent cut, with one exception. It does not require or allow rulemaking, public comment, hearings, advisory bodies, consultation with outside parties, or a right to sue. The phrase "determining such reasonable costs" might suggest an agency process, but the formula is spelled out in the statute itself, so no outside party takes part in any federal decision.

opus.b:
I'm labelling this section **No**: it involves no participation by anyone outside the federal government.

**The tempting reading:** "In determining such reasonable costs" could suggest an agency decision-making process, maybe even rulemaking. That fails here. The section only sets a fixed formula: allowable bad debts attributable to coinsurance are cut by 30 percent, except for individuals described in section 1935(c)(6)(A)(ii). Nothing in it calls for regulations, comment periods, hearings, consultation with outside parties, or a right to sue. Part (b) is just a technical fix to a cross-reference.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends the Social Security Act to define how reasonable costs for skilled nursing facilities are calculated, specifically regarding bad debts attributable to coinsurance amounts. It does not require consultation, coordination, or input from any outside parties (such as patients, providers, or the general public) before a decision is made. The reference to 'individuals who are entitled to benefits' is descriptive of the population affected by the cost calculation, not an invitation for their participation in the regulatory or administrative process.
qwen_chat.s: (a) In General.—Section 1861(v)(1) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1395x(v)(1)) is amended by adding at the end the following new subparagraph: “(V) In determining such reasonable costs for skilled nursing facilities with respect to cost reporting periods beginning on or after October 1, 2005, the amount of bad debts otherwise treated as allowed costs which are attributable to the coinsurance amounts under this title for individuals who are entitled to benefits under part A and—“(i) are not described in section 1935(c)(6)(A)(ii) shall be reduced by 30 percent of such amount otherwise allowable; and“(ii) are described in such section shall not be reduced.”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the statute affects "individuals who are entitled to benefits," it involves the public. However, the text merely defines how costs are calculated for reimbursement purposes; it does not require the government to consult with those individuals, nor does it grant them a role in the decision-making process. The definition explicitly excludes applications for benefits or grants, and this is a technical amendment to cost determination formulas, not a participatory mechanism.
